title: Accessibility, Localization & Adaptive UI
scopeHtml: Scope: VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, dark mode, theming, localization with string catalogs, size classes, iPad, right-to-left.

notes.title: Baseline and the adaptive mindset
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you handle accessibility with TalkBack and contentDescription, text scaling with sp, dark theme with values-night and Material theming, localization with strings.xml and values-xx, and screen sizes with window size classes and WindowManager. iOS has the same concerns with different tools: VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, asset catalog colors, String Catalogs, size classes and NavigationSplitView.

This track assumes Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials, with @Observable, NavigationStack, async/await and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (ObservableObject, NavigationView, XCTest, .strings files) are labelled as old-codebase material.

An iOS app is expected to be adaptive on five axes at once: user settings (text size, bold text, reduce motion, increase contrast, VoiceOver), appearance (light/dark, tint), language and region (strings, plurals, number/date formats, right-to-left), device and window (iPhone, iPad, split view, Stage Manager, landscape), and safe areas and input (notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator, keyboard). Apple reviews apps against the Human Interface Guidelines (HIG), and accessibility is also a legal requirement in many regions (for example the European Accessibility Act, in effect from June 2025 for many consumer products; verify applicability for your product).

Mapping:

Android iOS
TalkBack VoiceOver
contentDescription .accessibilityLabel
sp text units, font scale Dynamic Type, text styles, @ScaledMetric
values-night, Theme.Material3 Asset catalog light/dark variants, ColorScheme, tint
strings.xml, plurals String Catalog (.xcstrings), String(localized:)
Window size classes horizontalSizeClass / verticalSizeClass
ListDetailPaneScaffold NavigationSplitView
WindowInsets Safe area, safeAreaInset
HapticFeedback UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, .sensoryFeedback
Accessibility Scanner Xcode Accessibility Inspector, audit APIs

Real industry examples. Apple's own apps are the reference. Airbnb, Uber and Spotify publish accessibility commitments and ship VoiceOver-labelled UIs; Airbnb's engineering blog has described Dynamic Type and accessibility work in their design system.

Analogy. A well-built building has ramps, braille signs, adjustable lighting and signs in several languages from the start; retrofitting them later costs more and always misses some doors.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating accessibility, localization and dark mode as "polish" for later.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming a fixed font size in points like dp. iOS text should scale by text style.
  • Forgetting that every user setting is a test configuration, not an edge case.

notes.title: Accessibility basics: VoiceOver, labels, traits and values
notes.html:
Android equivalent. TalkBack reads contentDescription, labelFor, roles and AccessibilityNodeInfo. In Compose you use Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = ...; role = Role.Button }. In SwiftUI the accessibility tree is derived automatically from views, and you refine it with modifiers.

VoiceOver works by traversing accessibility elements, each with:

  • Label: what it is ("Add to cart").
  • Value: current state ("3", "50 percent").
  • Hint: what happens ("Opens the payment sheet"); optional and spoken after a pause.
  • Traits: role and behaviour (.isButton, .isHeader, .isSelected, .isImage, .updatesFrequently, .isLink).
  • Actions: custom actions, activate (double tap), increment/decrement (adjustable).
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Button {
    cart.add(product)
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "cart.badge.plus")
}
.accessibilityLabel("Add \(product.name) to cart")
.accessibilityHint("Adds one item and keeps you on this page")
IconButton(
    onClick = { cart.add(product) },
    modifier = Modifier.semantics {
        contentDescription = "Add ${product.name} to cart"
        onClick(label = "Adds one item and keeps you on this page") { false }
    }
) { Icon(Icons.Default.AddShoppingCart, contentDescription = null) }

Built-in controls (Button, Toggle, Slider, TextField, Text) are accessible by default. Common fixes:

  • Images: decorative images use Image(decorative: "bg") or .accessibilityHidden(true); meaningful images get .accessibilityLabel. SF Symbols have default labels, but they are generic and often wrong in context.
  • Grouping: combine a row into one element so VoiceOver does not make the user swipe through five pieces:
HStack {
    Image(systemName: "star.fill")
    Text(product.name)
    Text(product.priceText)
}
.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)     // reads "star, Shoes, 49 dollars" as one stop

Use .ignore plus your own label when the combined phrase reads poorly, and .contain when a container needs its own focus plus children.

  • Headers: .accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader) lets users jump by headings with the rotor, the analogue of TalkBack headings navigation.
  • Custom actions replace swipe-only gestures that VoiceOver cannot perform:
RowView(item: item)
    .swipeActions { Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { delete(item) } }
    .accessibilityAction(named: "Archive") { archive(item) }
  • Adjustable controls: .accessibilityAdjustableAction { direction in ... } for custom sliders and steppers.
  • Value for dynamic state: .accessibilityValue("\(Int(progress * 100)) percent").
  • Announcements: AccessibilityNotification.Announcement("Item added").post() (iOS 17+; older code uses UIAccessibility.post(notification: .announcement, argument:)) for non-focus changes such as toasts; .screenChanged / .layoutChanged move focus after navigation.
  • Focus control: @AccessibilityFocusState moves VoiceOver focus programmatically, for example to an error message after failed validation.
  • Touch targets: at least 44 x 44 points per HIG; Material suggests 48 dp. Use .frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44) and .contentShape(Rectangle()).
  • Order: .accessibilitySortPriority(_:) adjusts reading order when layout order does not match logical order.

UIKit equivalents (legacy code): isAccessibilityElement, accessibilityLabel, accessibilityTraits, accessibilityCustomActions, shouldGroupAccessibilityChildren, and UIAccessibility.post.

Other assistive technologies: Voice Control (needs visible labels matching spoken names, so .accessibilityInputLabels(["Add", "Add to cart"])), Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, Reduce Motion, Bold Text, Increase Contrast, Differentiate Without Color, Reduce Transparency. In SwiftUI read them via environment values: \.accessibilityReduceMotion, \.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor, \.accessibilityReduceTransparency, \.legibilityWeight, \.colorSchemeContrast.

struct Banner: View {
    @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
    @State private var visible = false

    var body: some View {
        Text("Saved")
            .opacity(visible ? 1 : 0)
            .animation(reduceMotion ? nil : .spring, value: visible)
    }
}

Testing. Xcode Accessibility Inspector (Xcode > Open Developer Tool) lets you hover over elements on Simulator or device, shows label/trait data, runs an audit that flags missing labels, small hit regions and contrast issues, and has a Settings panel to emulate Dynamic Type and other options. For automation, XCUITest performAccessibilityAudit() (Xcode 15+) runs the audit in UI tests (verify the API shape for your Xcode):

func testAccessibilityAudit() throws {
    let app = XCUIApplication()
    app.launch()
    try app.performAccessibilityAudit()      // fails on issues; filter with audit types if needed
}

Always test on a real device with VoiceOver on (triple-click side button shortcut), and with Android developers' habit corrected: VoiceOver gestures differ (swipe right/left to move, double tap to activate, three-finger swipe to scroll, two-finger twist for rotor).

Real examples. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and Airbnb's design system make labels, grouped rows and rotor headers part of component definitions, so teams get accessibility by default instead of per screen.

Analogy. VoiceOver is a tour guide reading a museum's placards: if the placard is missing, or five placards describe one painting, the visitor gets lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the element type in the label ("Cart button"). The trait already says "button".
  • Adding hints on everything; they are verbose and skippable by users.
  • Hiding purely decorative views incorrectly or leaving icon-only buttons unlabeled.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting importantForAccessibility; iOS uses accessibilityHidden and element grouping.

notes.title: Dynamic Type and scaled metrics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Users change font size in Settings; text in sp scales (Android 14 added non-linear font scaling up to 200 percent). iOS offers seven standard sizes plus five larger accessibility sizes (AX1 to AX5), and text styles that scale in a curve tuned per style.

Use text styles, not fixed sizes:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Order summary").font(.title2.bold())
    Text("Arrives Tuesday").font(.subheadline).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text(longDescription).font(.body)
}
Column {
    Text("Order summary", style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge)
    Text("Arrives Tuesday", style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
    Text(longDescription, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyLarge)
}

Text styles: .largeTitle, .title, .title2, .title3, .headline, .subheadline, .body, .callout, .footnote, .caption, .caption2. System fonts in these styles scale automatically. Custom fonts must opt in:

Text("Welcome").font(.custom("Avenir-Heavy", size: 28, relativeTo: .title))    // scales relative to .title

// UIKit (legacy):
// label.font = UIFontMetrics(forTextStyle: .title1).scaledFont(for: customFont)
// label.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true

Non-text sizes should scale too, with @ScaledMetric:

struct Avatar: View {
    @ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .body) private var size: CGFloat = 40
    var body: some View {
        Image("avatar").resizable().frame(width: size, height: size).clipShape(Circle())
    }
}

Design for the largest sizes (AX5 can make body text around three times larger than default; verify exact ratios):

  • Let text wrap (never lineLimit(1) on important text without a reason) and allow layout to grow vertically; avoid fixed heights.
  • Switch horizontal layouts to vertical at large sizes. ViewThatFits or the environment value dynamicTypeSize does it:
struct ActionRow: View {
    @Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var typeSize

    var body: some View {
        let layout = typeSize.isAccessibilitySize ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading)) : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())
        layout {
            Text("Total")
            Spacer()
            Text("$129.00").bold()
        }
    }
}

AnyLayout preserves view identity and state across the switch, which is better than an if/else of two stacks.

  • Cap sizes only when unavoidable (tab bars, navigation chrome): .dynamicTypeSize(...DynamicTypeSize.xxxLarge). Capping content text defeats the feature.
  • Scroll views: ensure every screen scrolls so large text is reachable (forms, onboarding, alerts with long text).
  • Minimum hit targets stay 44 points; icons next to text can use .imageScale and SF Symbols, which scale with the font.
  • Test with the Environment Overrides button in Xcode's debug bar (Dynamic Type slider, appearance, accessibility toggles), the Accessibility Inspector, and previews:
#Preview("Largest text") {
    CheckoutView()
        .dynamicTypeSize(.accessibility5)
}

Truncation behaviour is a frequent bug: Text truncates with an ellipsis by default when it runs out of space; use .fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true) to let text grow vertically when a parent constrains height, and .minimumScaleFactor(_:) sparingly (it fights users' size choice).

Real examples. Apple Mail and Messages reflow rows at accessibility sizes; Spotify and Uber ship adaptive layouts in their design systems where stacked variants replace row variants at large sizes.

Analogy. Dynamic Type is like a stretchy shirt rather than a fixed-size one: the garment (layout) must be designed to fit every wearer, not just the model.

Common interview traps.

  • Using .font(.system(size: 17)), which does not scale (it scales only with an explicit relative style).
  • Letting the layout break at AX sizes because a row of three items never wraps.
  • Capping Dynamic Type globally "to avoid layout bugs".
  • Android vs iOS: expecting sp to be enough; iOS wants semantic styles (.body, .headline), not raw numbers.

notes.title: Dark mode and theming
notes.html:
Android equivalent. values-night resources, isSystemInDarkTheme(), Material 3 color schemes and dynamic color. In iOS, semantic colors and asset-catalog color sets adapt automatically.

Rules:

  • Use semantic system colors: Color(.systemBackground), .primary, .secondary, Color(.secondarySystemBackground), Color(.separator), .accentColor/tint. They change between light and dark and between base and elevated levels.
  • Define brand colors in the Asset Catalog as color sets with Any / Dark (and optional high-contrast) variants; reference by name, or by generated symbols (Color.brandPrimary, Xcode 15+ generated asset symbols; verify setting name "Generate Swift Asset Symbol Extensions").
  • Do not hard-code Color.white/Color.black for backgrounds and text.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
extension Color {
    static let brandPrimary = Color("BrandPrimary")      // asset catalog: Any + Dark appearances
}

struct Card: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Text("Premium").font(.headline).foregroundStyle(.primary)
            Text("Billed monthly").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        .background(Color(.secondarySystemBackground), in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}
@Composable
fun Card() {
    Column(
        Modifier
            .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surfaceVariant, RoundedCornerShape(12.dp))
            .padding(16.dp)
    ) {
        Text("Premium", style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium, color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurface)
        Text("Billed monthly", color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant)
    }
}

Controlling the scheme:

  • Read: @Environment(\.colorScheme) var colorScheme (.light / .dark).
  • Force for a subtree: .preferredColorScheme(.dark) on the root or a presented view, or .environment(\.colorScheme, .dark) (affects environment value but not system controls consistently; prefer the former).
  • App-level theme setting stored in @AppStorage("appearance") and applied via .preferredColorScheme(...) at the root: nil means follow the system.
@main
struct ShopApp: App {
    @AppStorage("appearance") private var appearance: String = "system"

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView()
                .preferredColorScheme(appearance == "dark" ? .dark : appearance == "light" ? .light : nil)
                .tint(.brandPrimary)
        }
    }
}

Theming differences from Material: iOS has no global theme object like MaterialTheme. You get tint (.tint(_:)) for interactive accents, the environment for fonts and colors, and your own design-system layer (a Theme struct injected via .environment, or static extension tokens on Color and Font). Material 3 "dynamic color" from wallpaper has no iOS equivalent; users expect standard system components, not heavily custom skins.

Other appearance details:

  • Elevation in dark mode is shown by lighter surfaces (systemBackground vs secondarySystemBackground), not shadows alone.
  • Vibrancy and materials (.background(.ultraThinMaterial)) adapt automatically.
  • Images: provide dark variants in asset catalogs; template images tinted by foregroundStyle; SF Symbols adapt.
  • Contrast: WCAG 2.x text contrast ratios of 4.5:1 (normal text) and 3:1 (large text); provide a High Contrast variant for brand colors; read \.colorSchemeContrast.
  • iOS 18 added app icon variants (dark and tinted) and tintable controls; design the icon set with Any, Dark and Tinted appearances (verify in current HIG).
  • UIKit legacy: traitCollection.userInterfaceStyle, UIColor { trait in ... } dynamic providers, and traitCollectionDidChange(_:) (deprecated in iOS 17 in favour of registerForTraitChanges); CGColor values on layers do not update automatically, so refresh layer colors on trait change.
// UIKit iOS 17+: observe trait changes
registerForTraitChanges([UITraitUserInterfaceStyle.self]) { (self: Self, _) in
    self.layer.borderColor = UIColor.separator.cgColor
}

Real examples. Apple's guidelines emphasise semantic colors; large apps (Slack, Twitter/X, Spotify) maintain named color tokens that map to light/dark/high-contrast sets in an asset catalog, enabling designers to change tokens without engineers editing views.

Analogy. Semantic colors are like giving paint names ("wall", "trim") instead of exact codes: the decorator can repaint the whole house for night without you rewriting the instructions.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-coded Color.white/.black or hex values with no dark variant.
  • Storing CGColor on layers and forgetting to update on appearance change.
  • Forcing dark mode for the whole app because "our brand looks better dark", without a user option.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting a single theme resource file; iOS combines asset catalogs, environment values and tint.

notes.title: Localization with String Catalogs
notes.html:
Android equivalent. res/values/strings.xml, values-fr/strings.xml, <plurals>, getString(R.string.x, arg), and Locale-aware formatters. iOS uses String Catalogs (.xcstrings, Xcode 15+) that replace .strings and .stringsdict files in new projects.

A String Catalog is a single JSON-backed file edited in a table UI. Xcode extracts string keys automatically from your code at build time, tracks translation state (New, Needs Review, Stale, Translated), and supports plural variations and device-specific variations.

How SwiftUI picks up strings:

  • Text("Welcome") with a string literal is a LocalizedStringKey; the literal is the key and is looked up in the catalog automatically.
  • Text(verbatim: "ABC-123") opts out of localization (IDs, codes).
  • For a String variable, use String(localized: "Welcome back") (not NSLocalizedString, which you will meet in old codebases) or LocalizedStringResource.
  • Use comment: for translators: String(localized: "Save", comment: "Button that saves the draft").
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Interpolation becomes a format argument in the catalog: "Hello, %@"
Text("Hello, \(user.name)")

// Plural: define variations for "%lld items" in the catalog (one, other, plus few/many for languages that need them)
Text("\(count) items")

// Outside views
let title = String(localized: "Order placed", comment: "Confirmation title")
// strings.xml
// <string name="greeting">Hello, %1$s</string>
// <plurals name="items"><item quantity="one">%d item</item><item quantity="other">%d items</item></plurals>
Text(stringResource(R.string.greeting, user.name))
Text(pluralStringResource(R.plurals.items, count, count))
val title = context.getString(R.string.order_placed)

Plural rules follow CLDR categories (zero, one, two, few, many, other); Arabic has all six, Russian has one/few/many/other. Always define the variations the language requires, never concatenate "item" + "s".

Formatting numbers, currency, dates, units uses the locale-aware FormatStyle APIs, not manual string building:

let price = 1234.5.formatted(.currency(code: "EUR"))              // "€1,234.50" or "1.234,50 €" by locale
let date = Date.now.formatted(date: .abbreviated, time: .shortened)
let distance = Measurement(value: 5, unit: UnitLength.kilometers).formatted()  // converts to miles for US locale
let list = ["Apples", "Pears", "Plums"].formatted()                // "Apples, Pears, and Plums" (locale-aware)

Because DateFormatter and NumberFormatter are expensive to create (see the performance note on formatters), prefer .formatted() or cache instances.

Operational practices:

  • Pseudolanguages in the scheme (Run options > App Language: Double-Length Pseudolanguage, Right-to-Left Pseudolanguage, Accented Pseudolanguage) test truncation and RTL without real translations.
  • Export/import localizations: Product > Export Localizations produces .xcloc bundles for translators; the String Catalog is also easy to send to services (Lokalise, Phrase, Crowdin integrate).
  • Localize beyond strings: images with text in the asset catalog (language variants), InfoPlist.xcstrings for permission descriptions and the app display name, App Store metadata in App Store Connect per language.
  • Bundle and locale selection: the app language follows the system's per-app language setting (Settings > App > Language, iOS 13+). Avoid building your own in-app language switcher unless required; if you must, use the per-app system setting link.
  • Locale.current, Locale.preferredLanguages, Bundle.main.preferredLocalizations expose the choice.
  • Testing: set .environment(\.locale, Locale(identifier: "ar")) in previews:
#Preview("Arabic RTL") {
    CheckoutView()
        .environment(\.locale, Locale(identifier: "ar"))
        .environment(\.layoutDirection, .rightToLeft)
}

Right-to-left (RTL). SwiftUI mirrors layout automatically: HStack reverses, .leading/.trailing replace left/right, and many SF Symbols flip when marked as such. Rules:

  • Use .padding(.leading) and alignment: .leading, never .left/.right (UIKit: leadingAnchor/trailingAnchor, not leftAnchor).
  • Do not mirror content that is not directional: logos, media playback controls, numbers, clocks, and charts' time axes usually remain unchanged. For custom images that should flip, use .flipsForRightToLeftLayoutDirection(true).
  • Mixed-direction text (English product names inside Arabic) is handled by the Unicode bidi algorithm; test with real strings.
  • Read \.layoutDirection for logic that depends on direction.

Real examples. Airbnb, Booking.com and Uber operate in dozens of locales and run pseudolocalization in CI to catch truncation; Duolingo and WhatsApp rely on plural and gender-correct strings maintained through translation platforms.

Analogy. A String Catalog is a restaurant menu with one master dish list and a column per language; the kitchen (your code) orders by dish ID, never by hard-coded English names.

Common interview traps.

  • Concatenating strings ("You have " + n + " items"), which breaks grammar and word order.
  • Using String(format:) with %d for Int on 64-bit when the catalog expects %lld.
  • Hard-coding .left/.right and leaving RTL broken.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting R.string generated IDs; iOS uses the literal or LocalizedStringResource and Xcode symbol generation for catalogs (verify "Generate String Catalog Symbols" in recent Xcode).

notes.title: Size classes, iPad and multitasking
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Window size classes (compact, medium, expanded), WindowInfoTracker, foldable and tablet layouts, ListDetailPaneScaffold, and multi-window. iOS expresses coarse space with size classes per axis and fine space with actual geometry.

Size classes are .compact or .regular per axis, from @Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) and \.verticalSizeClass:

Device and state Horizontal Vertical
iPhone portrait compact regular
iPhone landscape (most) compact (Pro Max / Plus: regular) compact
iPad full screen regular regular
iPad Split View / Slide Over (narrow) compact regular

The table is a summary; exact values depend on device and window width (verify on current devices). The main lesson: do not use UIDevice.current.userInterfaceIdiom == .pad to decide layout. A full-screen iPad and a narrow iPad Slide Over window need different layouts; size classes and available width capture that.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct ProductDetail: View {
    @Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) private var hSize

    var body: some View {
        if hSize == .compact {
            VStack { gallery; info }
        } else {
            HStack(alignment: .top) { gallery; info }
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun ProductDetail(windowSizeClass: WindowSizeClass) {
    if (windowSizeClass.widthSizeClass == WindowWidthSizeClass.Compact) {
        Column { Gallery(); Info() }
    } else {
        Row { Gallery(); Info() }
    }
}

Better in many cases: use self-adapting layouts so you avoid explicit branching: ViewThatFits, Grid with LazyVGrid(columns: [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 160))]), and the Layout protocol (see also: SwiftUI Fundamentals).

Adaptive navigation with NavigationSplitView (iOS 16+). It shows a two- or three-column sidebar / content / detail layout on regular width and collapses to a stack on compact width automatically, the analogue of Android's list-detail pane scaffold.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct MailRoot: View {
    @State private var selectedFolder: Folder?
    @State private var selectedMessage: Message?
    @State private var columnVisibility: NavigationSplitViewVisibility = .automatic

    var body: some View {
        NavigationSplitView(columnVisibility: $columnVisibility) {
            List(Folder.all, selection: $selectedFolder) { folder in
                Label(folder.name, systemImage: folder.icon)
            }
            .navigationTitle("Mailboxes")
        } content: {
            if let folder = selectedFolder {
                MessageList(folder: folder, selection: $selectedMessage)
            } else {
                ContentUnavailableView("Select a folder", systemImage: "tray")
            }
        } detail: {
            if let message = selectedMessage {
                MessageDetail(message: message)
            } else {
                ContentUnavailableView("Select a message", systemImage: "envelope")
            }
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun MailRoot() {
    val navigator = rememberListDetailPaneScaffoldNavigator<Message>()
    ListDetailPaneScaffold(
        directive = navigator.scaffoldDirective,
        value = navigator.scaffoldValue,
        listPane = { AnimatedPane { MessageList(onSelect = { navigator.navigateTo(ListDetailPaneScaffoldRole.Detail, it) }) } },
        detailPane = { AnimatedPane { navigator.currentDestination?.content?.let { MessageDetail(it) } } }
    )
}

ContentUnavailableView is iOS 17+. For iPad-style tab bars, iOS 18 introduced a new TabView style that shows a floating tab bar convertible to a sidebar via Tab and .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable) (verify the API in current docs).

iPad specifics:

  • Multitasking: Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager (resizable windows, iPadOS 16+), and multiple scenes (WindowGroup supports multiple windows; handle state per scene with @SceneStorage). Apps must support resizing and should not assume device orientation or screen size; Apple requires iPad apps to support all multitasking unless opting out via UIRequiresFullScreen (deprecated in iOS 26 era; verify).
  • Pointer and keyboard: .hoverEffect, .keyboardShortcut, menu bar commands (.commands { CommandMenu("Edit") { ... } }), context menus.
  • Drag and drop between apps and windows, Transferable protocol with .draggable and .dropDestination.
  • Pencil input and PencilKit for drawing apps.
  • Popover presentations on iPad where a sheet appears on iPhone (an action sheet needs a source anchor).
  • Do not scale up the phone UI: use sidebars, multi-column layouts and readable content width (.frame(maxWidth: 700) for forms; readableContentGuide in UIKit).
  • Previews: #Preview(traits: .landscapeLeft) and device selection in Xcode canvas.

If you support iPad, test in portrait and landscape at all multitasking widths; if your app is iPhone-only it runs scaled on iPad, which App Review accepts but looks bad, so decide deliberately (TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY).

Real examples. Apple Mail and Notes show the canonical three-column split; Slack, Spotify and Airbnb use sidebar or two-pane layouts on iPad; Facebook and Instagram originally shipped iPhone layouts scaled on iPad for years, which users complained about.

Analogy. Size classes are like clothing sizes (S/M/L): coarse buckets for choosing the pattern, while geometry readers are the tailor's exact tape measure.

Common interview traps.

  • Branching on device idiom instead of size class or width.
  • Forgetting that iPhone landscape can be regular width on large models.
  • Assuming a sheet is correct on iPad without checking popover presentation and size.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting resource qualifiers like layout-sw600dp; iOS decides in code with size classes and adaptive containers.

notes.title: Human Interface Guidelines: what Android developers must unlearn
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Material Design guidelines. The HIG is Apple's equivalent, and App Review can reject apps that violate certain parts (for example, using system UI misleadingly, or custom back behaviour that traps users, plus requirements around Sign in with Apple when offering third-party logins, verify current rule text).

Key differences from Material habits:

Android habit iOS expectation
Floating Action Button Primary action in the navigation bar (top right "+"), toolbar, or inline button; FAB is not an iOS idiom
Hardware/system Back button No back button; swipe from the left edge and navigation bar back button; never break the swipe-back gesture
Navigation drawer (hamburger) Tab bar at the bottom (up to 5 tabs); sidebar on iPad
Top app bar with overflow menu "three dots" Toolbar buttons, Menu, context menus (long press)
Snackbar Inline status, banners, alerts for important cases; no standard snackbar (toast-like patterns are custom)
Material dialogs with right-aligned buttons alert with stacked/side-by-side buttons; destructive role in red; action sheets (confirmationDialog)
Bottom sheets (modal) Sheets with detents (.presentationDetents([.medium, .large])), grabber
Ripple effect Subtle highlight/opacity change, no ripple
Roboto, sp text San Francisco (system font), Dynamic Type text styles
Toggle switches & radio buttons Toggle, Picker (menu, segmented, wheel), checkmarks in lists
Text buttons in caps Sentence case, tinted text buttons, borders optional
Settings in-app screen Settings bundle or in-app; permissions in system Settings
Back stack with onBackPressed Swipe back plus interactiveDismissDisabled only when truly needed
Share via Intent chooser ShareLink / UIActivityViewController share sheet
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Modern sheet with detents (iOS 16+)
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FiltersView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
}

// Destructive confirmation as an action sheet-like dialog
.confirmationDialog("Delete this note?", isPresented: $confirmDelete, titleVisibility: .visible) {
    Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { delete() }
    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { }
}
ModalBottomSheet(onDismissRequest = { showFilters = false }) { FiltersView() }

AlertDialog(
    onDismissRequest = { confirmDelete = false },
    title = { Text("Delete this note?") },
    confirmButton = { TextButton(onClick = { delete() }) { Text("Delete") } },
    dismissButton = { TextButton(onClick = { confirmDelete = false }) { Text("Cancel") } }
)

More HIG essentials:

  • Large titles in navigation bars that collapse on scroll (.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.large)).
  • SF Symbols (thousands of icons that match text weight and scale) instead of bundling many icon PNGs.
  • System controls first: prefer Button, Toggle, DatePicker, Menu; they inherit accessibility, Dynamic Type, localization and OS-level visual updates (such as the iOS 26 design refresh, "Liquid Glass"; verify details), whereas custom controls must reimplement everything.
  • Permissions: ask in context, just in time, with a clear purpose string in Info.plist (NSCameraUsageDescription etc.); missing strings crash the app on access. Denied permissions lead users to Settings, which you can open with UIApplication.openSettingsURLString.
  • Gestures: do not override system gestures (edge swipe back, control center, home indicator swipe); avoid hiding essential actions behind unusual gestures.
  • Spacing and margins: respect safe area and standard 16 to 20 point margins; use system padding (.padding()) which adapts.
  • Onboarding and splash: no fake splash; keep launch screen static and onboarding short; avoid asking to rate the app at launch (requestReview is rate-limited by the system).
  • Review risk: apps that look like web wrappers with no native value (guideline 4.2 minimum functionality), external payment links for digital goods (see StoreKit rules, verify regional changes), and missing account deletion in apps that allow account creation.

Real examples. Apps that ported Android UI directly, such as early Google apps on iOS, were criticised and later adopted native patterns; Airbnb, Spotify and Uber use iOS tab bars and native sheets while keeping brand identity in color, imagery and typography accents.

Analogy. Moving countries: driving on the other side of the road is not wrong, it is the local rule everyone else relies on; follow it so people do not crash into you.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding a FAB or hamburger drawer and calling it done.
  • Intercepting or disabling the interactive pop gesture.
  • Using a snackbar-like toast for errors that need action.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting a global back button; navigation correctness depends on the nav bar and swipe, and deep-link flows must still allow dismiss/back.

notes.title: Safe areas, keyboard handling and haptics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Edge-to-edge with WindowInsets (systemBars, ime, displayCutout), imePadding(), windowSoftInputMode, and HapticFeedback/VibrationEffect. iOS has safe areas, keyboard avoidance built into SwiftUI, and Core Haptics wrappers.

Safe areas. SwiftUI lays content inside the safe area by default (below status bar / Dynamic Island, above home indicator). Extend backgrounds under unsafe regions with .ignoresSafeArea() while keeping content inside:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
ZStack {
    Color.brandPrimary.ignoresSafeArea()          // background goes edge to edge
    VStack { Text("Welcome"); Spacer() }          // content respects safe area
}

// Pin a bottom bar above the home indicator and keyboard
.safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom) {
    Button("Checkout") { checkout() }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        .padding()
        .background(.bar)
}
Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize().background(BrandPrimary)) {
    Column(Modifier.windowInsetsPadding(WindowInsets.safeDrawing)) { Text("Welcome") }
    Button(
        onClick = ::checkout,
        modifier = Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomCenter).navigationBarsPadding().imePadding()
    ) { Text("Checkout") }
}

safeAreaInset(edge:) (iOS 15+) adds content to the safe area so scroll views inset automatically, which is the SwiftUI way to build sticky bottom bars. Avoid hard-coding top inset numbers (the Dynamic Island, notch and status bar heights vary by device). Read insets only when needed with GeometryReader (proxy.safeAreaInsets); in UIKit, view.safeAreaInsets and safeAreaLayoutGuide.

Keyboard handling. SwiftUI resizes the safe area for the software keyboard (the keyboard safe area region) so scrollable content and safeAreaInset bars move up automatically. Useful tools:

  • .scrollDismissesKeyboard(.interactively) (iOS 16+) to dismiss on scroll; .immediately and .never also exist.
  • @FocusState to move focus between fields and to dismiss:
struct LoginForm: View {
    enum Field: Hashable { case email, password }
    @FocusState private var focus: Field?
    @State private var email = ""
    @State private var password = ""

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Email", text: $email)
                .textContentType(.emailAddress)
                .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
                .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
                .focused($focus, equals: .email)
                .submitLabel(.next)
                .onSubmit { focus = .password }
            SecureField("Password", text: $password)
                .textContentType(.password)
                .focused($focus, equals: .password)
                .submitLabel(.go)
                .onSubmit { submit() }
        }
        .toolbar {
            ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .keyboard) {
                Spacer()
                Button("Done") { focus = nil }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • textContentType enables AutoFill (passwords, one-time codes .oneTimeCode, addresses) and iCloud Keychain; it improves conversion and is also an accessibility win.
  • To ignore automatic avoidance: .ignoresSafeArea(.keyboard).
  • UIKit legacy: observe UIResponder.keyboardWillChangeFrameNotification and adjust constraints or scroll insets; or use keyboardLayoutGuide (iOS 15+) to pin views to the keyboard.

Haptics. Haptic feedback should confirm actions and never be decorative noise.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// SwiftUI iOS 17+
Button("Add") { add() }
    .sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: itemCount)

// UIKit generators (works everywhere)
let generator = UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(style: .medium)
generator.prepare()                 // reduces latency
generator.impactOccurred()

let notifier = UINotificationFeedbackGenerator()
notifier.notificationOccurred(.success)
val haptics = LocalHapticFeedback.current
Button(onClick = {
    haptics.performHapticFeedback(HapticFeedbackType.LongPress)
    add()
}) { Text("Add") }

Kinds: impact (light, medium, heavy, soft, rigid), selection (UISelectionFeedbackGenerator for pickers), notification (success, warning, error). CoreHaptics (CHHapticEngine) is for custom patterns on supported devices (iPhone 8+ for Taptic Engine; iPad has no haptics; the Simulator does nothing, so test on device). Respect system settings: haptics are disabled when the user turns off System Haptics, and avoid overuse in accessibility contexts. Pair haptics with visual and audio cues, never as the only signal.

Real examples. Apple Pay confirmation, pull-to-refresh and picker ticks are canonical haptic uses; Uber and Instagram use light impacts for taps like like/reactions; keyboard accessory bars with "Done" are standard in forms apps.

Analogy. Safe areas are like the margins on a printed page: backgrounds may bleed to the edge, but text stays inside so the printer's grip (notch, home indicator) never cuts it off.

Common interview traps.

  • Using hard-coded 44 or 20 point top paddings for the status bar/notch.
  • Ignoring .ignoresSafeArea order or applying it to the wrong view and pushing content under the island.
  • Missing textContentType so password managers cannot autofill.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting windowSoftInputMode=adjustResize; SwiftUI avoids the keyboard automatically but UIKit legacy needs manual handling.

notes.title: Accessibility, localization and adaptive UI in production
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The same checklist you run before an Android release: TalkBack pass, font scale 200 percent, dark theme, RTL pseudolocale, tablet emulator, Pre-launch report.

A practical pre-release checklist for an iOS screen:

  1. VoiceOver pass on device: every control reachable, labelled, in a logical order, no duplicate or empty stops, custom gestures have alternatives.
  2. Dynamic Type: test default, XXXL and AX5; layouts reflow, nothing clipped, scrolling works.
  3. Appearance: light, dark, Increase Contrast, Reduce Transparency, Bold Text, Reduce Motion, Differentiate Without Color.
  4. Language: pseudolanguages (double-length, accented, RTL), plurals, dates, currencies; a real RTL language such as Arabic or Hebrew.
  5. Devices: smallest supported iPhone (e.g., SE class), Pro Max, iPad portrait/landscape, Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager.
  6. Input: keyboard (hardware and software), AutoFill, Voice Control, Switch Control, pointer.
  7. Automation: performAccessibilityAudit() in UI tests, snapshot tests over a matrix (swift-snapshot-testing from Point-Free) covering dark mode, large text and locales.
import SnapshotTesting
import SwiftUI
import Testing

@MainActor
struct CheckoutSnapshotTests {
    @Test(arguments: [DynamicTypeSize.large, .accessibility3], [ColorScheme.light, .dark])
    func checkout(size: DynamicTypeSize, scheme: ColorScheme) {
        let view = CheckoutView(model: .fixture)
            .dynamicTypeSize(size)
            .environment(\.colorScheme, scheme)
        // assertSnapshot API: verify the exact strategy for SwiftUI views in your snapshot-testing version
        assertSnapshot(of: UIHostingController(rootView: view), as: .image(on: .iPhone13))
    }
}

(Swift Testing and swift-snapshot-testing interplay requires a recent version of the library; verify.)

Common production incidents:

  • Truncated price or CTA at AX sizes because of fixed heights, leading to support tickets from low-vision users.
  • App Review or legal complaint about missing VoiceOver labels on the checkout button.
  • Dark mode flash: a hard-coded white background for web content or launch screen, because the launch screen did not have dark variants.
  • Wrong plural or grammar in a language with several plural forms; or the app shows English fallback because the catalog marked a key "stale" and not shipped.
  • RTL bug: an arrow icon pointing the wrong way, or a progress bar filling from the wrong side.
  • iPad crash on share sheet presented without a sourceView/popover anchor in legacy UIKit code (UIActivityViewController on iPad needs popoverPresentationController?.sourceView); ShareLink handles it automatically.
  • Keyboard covering a bottom button in a UIKit screen using manual constraints.

Design system tip: build accessibility into reusable components (PrimaryButton, FormField, PriceLabel) once. Pull colors, fonts, spacing and strings from tokens, apply ScaledMetric and minimum hit areas inside the component, and screens inherit correctness. This is the approach large teams (Airbnb DLS, Spotify Encore, Uber Base) take.

Analogy. Pre-flight checklist: pilots do not rely on memory, they walk the same list before every takeoff, and the aircraft gets safer even when the crew changes.

Common interview traps.

  • Only testing on one simulator in light mode and English.
  • Claiming accessibility is "someone else's job" instead of describing how you build it into components and tests.
  • Forgetting that screenshot tests of text-heavy screens must run at several text sizes and locales.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Accessibility, localization and adaptivity are built in from day one on iOS and are verified in Xcode Accessibility Inspector, Environment Overrides, previews and UI tests.
  • VoiceOver reads label, value, trait and hint; group rows with .accessibilityElement(children: .combine), mark headers, add custom actions, keep 44 point targets, and respect Reduce Motion and other environment values.
  • Dynamic Type: use text styles, Font.custom(_:size:relativeTo:), @ScaledMetric, wrapping layouts, and switch to vertical layout at accessibility sizes using AnyLayout or ViewThatFits; do not fix font sizes.
  • Dark mode: semantic colors and asset-catalog color sets with dark and high-contrast variants; theming uses tint, environment and a token layer, not a Material-style global theme.
  • Localization: String Catalogs (.xcstrings), String(localized:), plural variations by CLDR category, FormatStyle formatting, pseudolanguages, and automatic RTL mirroring with leading/trailing.
  • Adaptive UI: size classes plus geometry, NavigationSplitView for list-detail, iPad multitasking and multiple windows; never branch on device idiom alone.
  • HIG: tab bar not drawer, no FAB, swipe-back preserved, sheets with detents, confirmation dialogs, system controls and SF Symbols, permissions in context.
  • Safe areas via .ignoresSafeArea for backgrounds and safeAreaInset for sticky bars; keyboard avoidance is automatic in SwiftUI, with @FocusState, scrollDismissesKeyboard and textContentType for forms; haptics via .sensoryFeedback or feedback generators.
  • Items marked verify: European Accessibility Act applicability, performAccessibilityAudit() shape, size-class table values, iOS 18 TabView sidebar-adaptable API, UIRequiresFullScreen status, Liquid Glass details, string catalog symbol generation, snapshot-testing integration with Swift Testing.
